newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Top EU officials tackle tax competition.
newsitem.headline: Top EU officials tackle tax competition.

text.p: Senior EU government officials discussed on Tuesday ways to crack down on unfair tax competition and tax evasion.
The debate on the need to bring national savings and corporate tax schemes closer together has heated up in the run up to the European single currency due to be launched in 1999.

Finance ministers in France, Germany and Belgium called in January for a reduction in tax disparities, concerned that the abolition of exchange rate risk in monetary union will further encourage savers and companies to shift their investments around the bloc in search of the most favourable tax regimes.

A group of personal representatives of finance ministers discussed on Tuesday how different taxation levels were harming national budgets, working from a European Commission document outlining options for a future code of conduct, Commission officials said.
The Commission will prepare a more detailed version of a possible code before the group's next meeting in June, they added.
Sweden's minister for fiscal affairs Thomas Ostros, one of the few ministers to attend the meeting, said the debate focused on savings, energy and corporate taxes.
"The discussion has made progress and there is a fairly positive attitude among most member states," he told Reuters after the meeting.

Despite the increasing awareness that different tax rates constitute unfair competition -- considered incompatible with the end of controls on capital movements in 1993 and with a single currency -- there is little hope for an EU-wide tax area.
This is because decisions on tax issues require the approval of all EU 15 states.
But European Taxation Commissioner Mario Monti said last week that the Commission would again propose binding rules on a minimum savings tax. A similar proposal was rejected in 1994.

"The idea would be to work on a package of measures (legislative and non-legislative) instead of focusing on a single step approach," the Commission said in a statement on Tuesday after the taxation meeting.
Luxembourg has always opposed an EU-wide minimum withholding tax on capital income, a position largely supported by Britain.
Germany and Belgium, on the other hand, strongly support such a move in the face of massive tax evasion due to the favourable tax regime in the neighbouring Grand Duchy.

The group's representatives also include French Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure and his counterpart in Luxembourg, Marc Fischbach. The new British government sent director for budget and public finance Paul Gray.

The high-level taxation group, created in December 1996, will meet for the third time just ahead of next month's EU summit in Amsterdam, which is expected to discuss the issue in as part of a debate on completing the bloc's border-free market.
